topics.title: Employment: people, participation and measurement
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Separate the labour force, workers and unemployed before interpreting a rate. This pilot covers selected concepts, not the entire unemployment chapter.

nodes.label: Employment measurement
Labour force: employed plus unemployed
LFPR: labour force / population
Workforce: those actually employed
Unemployment rate: unemployed / labour force
Underemployment: work below skill or education level (notes' example)

cells: LFPR
Labour force
Population of the defined group
Do not switch age group or reference period in a comparison.
Workforce participation rate
Employed people
Population of the defined group
Employment is not the same as labour-force membership.
Unemployment rate
Unemployed people
Labour force of the defined group
The denominator is not the entire population.

tables.title: Diagnose the employment constraint before choosing a policy

cells: Seasonal
Work disappears in predictable parts of a production calendar.
Consider off-season livelihood diversification, not only vacancy information.
Disguised
Removing a redundant worker need not reduce output.
Enable productive non-farm work; counting everyone as working can hide low productivity.
Structural
Skills, geography or the production structure do not match labour demand.
Match training and mobility support to actual vacancies; demand support alone may not resolve mismatch.
Frictional
Temporary search and movement between jobs.
Improve information and matching rather than classify every search spell as a permanent skills deficit.
Cyclical
Economy-wide weakness reduces demand for workers.
Diagnose the demand downturn; distinguish it from predictable seasonality.

cards.question: Illustrative calculation: population 1,000; labour force 600; employed 540. Find LFPR and unemployment rate.
cards.answer: LFPR = 600/1,000 = 60%. Unemployed = 600 - 540 = 60; unemployment rate = 60/600 = 10%. The numbers are invented for practice, not observed labour statistics.

cards.question: Are everyone in the labour force and everyone employed the same set?
cards.answer: No. Labour force includes employed and unemployed people; workforce refers to the employed.

cards.question: Illustrative case: labour force falls from 500 to 450 while employed stays 400. Does falling unemployment prove more jobs?
cards.answer: Initially UR = (500 - 400)/500 = 20%; later UR = (450 - 400)/450 ≈ 11.1%. No new job appears. Participation has fallen, so read LFPR and WPR alongside UR. The invented example holds the underlying population constant.

cards.question: Illustrative case: six farm workers produce the same output as four. Is that the same as having no work after harvest?
cards.answer: No. The first is a stylised disguised-unemployment case: some labour is redundant. The second is seasonal unemployment. Their causes and remedies differ even if both reflect underused labour.

cards.question: Why should rates not be compared without their reference-period definitions?
cards.answer: A usual-status lens and a weekly or daily lens can capture different work patterns. The notes' exact classification wording contains inconsistencies, so use this distinction conceptually and verify official PLFS rules before quoting thresholds.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Employment-centred growth requires more than a low unemployment rate.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: define labour force/workforce and rate denominators → contrast participation with unemployment → diagnose seasonal, disguised, structural or cyclical constraints → match job creation, skills and matching policies to causes → discuss work quality and underemployment → evaluate with multiple indicators and consistent reference periods.

cards.question: What is the expanded depth goal for this existing employment packet?
cards.answer: Retain the original measurement map; add denominator fluency, unemployment diagnosis and mechanism-led policy evaluation. Practise a rate case and a balanced descriptive plan. Do not memorise erroneous UPS/UPSS wording, assume a lower UR always means more work, or rely on unverified law-replacement claims.

cards.question: Illustrative case: vacancies require technical skills, while applicants lack them. Why might a general spending boost be insufficient?
cards.answer: The stated constraint is structural mismatch. A defensible response links demand for specific skills to training and access to suitable jobs; merely expanding spending does not guarantee applicants can fill those positions.

topics.title: Motivation: diagnose the broken link
topics.subject: Management
topics.summary: Compare what motivates an employee with how motivation works. Apply theory to a case instead of memorising author names alone.

nodes.label: Motivation: needs and decision processes
Content theories ask what motivates
Process theories ask how motivation occurs
Herzberg: hygiene factors versus motivators
Vroom: expectancy, instrumentality, valence
Adams: perceived fairness of treatment

cells: Expectancy
Can my effort produce the required performance?
Training, resources and feasible targets.
Instrumentality
Will performance actually produce the reward?
Credible, transparent performance-to-reward decisions.
Valence
Do I value this reward?
Discover what this employee values instead of assuming all want the same reward.
Herzberg
Job conditions versus intrinsic achievement/growth
Removing a source of dissatisfaction is not identical to adding a motivator.
Vroom
A weak link between effort, performance and a valued outcome
Reward value alone does not establish a credible performance-to-reward link.
Adams
Perceived unfairness in organisational treatment
Fairness is a perception to investigate, not simply identical pay for everyone.

cards.question: Illustrative case: an employee wants promotion but thinks selection ignores performance. Diagnose the weak Vroom component.
cards.answer: Instrumentality: the employee does not believe performance will produce the desired reward. A credible selection process addresses this link; a larger reward alone may not.

cards.question: Change the case: selection is fair, but the employee doubts they can meet the target. What changed?
cards.answer: The weak link is expectancy: effort is not expected to yield the required performance. Consider ability, support and target feasibility.

topics.title: Digital rupee: programmability and payment use
topics.subject: Finance
topics.summary: Use the monthly item to distinguish scheduling a payment from restricting its purpose. Product-launch claims below are from the supplied compilation, not an official verification.

nodes.label: Digital rupee: reported product features
Scheduled transfers: amount and frequency
Purpose controls: permitted spending categories
Reported institution: Bank of India; technology partner: Montran India

tables.title: Compare the function, not just the acronym

cells: Scheduled transfer
When and how much is transferred
Is a recurring monthly transfer automatically a spending restriction? No.
Purpose-based controls
Permitted uses after receipt
Can the recipient spend funds outside the permitted category? Check the applicable restriction.

cards.question: Illustrative case: funds may be spent only on tuition. Is this merely a recurring transfer?
cards.answer: No. It illustrates a purpose restriction. A schedule concerns timing/frequency, not necessarily how the recipient may spend the funds.

facts.label: Institution named in the compilation's programmability item

observations.value: Bank of India; platform developed by Montran India (compilation claim; verify official launch and scope).
observations.as_of: October 2026 compilation; event date not independently verified

updates.title: Compilation reports programmable digital-rupee features
updates.body: The October compilation attributes scheduled CBDC-wallet transfers and purpose-based spending controls to a Bank of India product. Link this to payment design; verify the bank/RBI release before memorising launch details. This is a selected item, not full monthly finance coverage.

topics.title: Forest certification: news to static concepts
topics.subject: GA
topics.summary: Organise a certification item by scheme, purpose, recipient and verification need rather than collecting an isolated headline.

nodes.label: PRAMAAN / IFWCS: compilation's certification item
Indian Forest and Wood Certification Scheme
Sourcing and forest-management assurance
Reported recipients include APFDC and a bamboo farmer

cells: Framework
IFWCS; certificates described as PRAMAAN
Official scheme name, owner and certification scope.
Purpose
Forest-management and sourcing requirements
Which standards and product categories are covered?
Reported development
Certificates awarded to forest/bamboo participants
Event date and any 'first' claim in the official release.

cards.question: What five fields would you retrieve for a certification news item?
cards.answer: What changed; the scheme/issuer; covered product or beneficiary; standard/conditions; event date and source. Do not equate certification automatically with a subsidy or cash transfer.

updates.title: Forest-certification item in the October compilation
updates.body: The source describes PRAMAAN certificates under IFWCS. Use this as a bridge to forest management and sustainable sourcing. The reported award details and 'first' claim still need official confirmation; the month here denotes the compilation edition.

topics.title: Growth forecasts: publisher, period and revision
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Attach every forecast to its publisher, release and reference period. Different institutions' forecasts are not automatically conflicting observations of the same fact.

nodes.label: GDP forecast: a dated estimate, not an actual outcome
Publisher/report: World Bank versus IMF
Reference period: fiscal year versus calendar year
Revision: compare the same institution and forecast period
Growth drivers and risks: industry, services, agriculture and demand

tables.title: What the supplied October compilation reports (unverified)

cells: World Bank / South Asia Economic Update
Compilation claim; verify the original report, not only the monthly table.
IMF / World Economic Outlook
A different publisher: not an automatic contradiction of the World Bank forecast.

cards.question: One report shows 7.1% and another 7.0%. Must one be wrong?
cards.answer: No. Check institution, release date, forecast horizon, fiscal/calendar basis and method. Different institutions can publish different forecasts. Verify the figures against original releases before memorising.

cards.question: Application prompt: does a growth forecast alone prove broad employment improvement?
cards.answer: No. A GDP forecast is not a labour-force measure. Support an employment claim with relevant labour data and its reference period. This is an analytical link between the two sample topics, not a quoted claim from the compilation.

facts.label: World Bank India FY 2026-27 real GDP forecast

observations.value: 7.1% (as reported by the supplied compilation; original report not verified)

facts.label: IMF India FY 2026-27 real GDP forecast

observations.value: 7.0% (as reported by the supplied compilation; original report not verified)

updates.title: October growth-forecast comparison
updates.body: The supplied compilation reports India forecasts from the World Bank and IMF. Keep the two publisher-specific fact records separate. Link growth mechanisms to ESI, while using labour data rather than GDP alone for employment conclusions. This pilot covers only one selected economic-current-affairs item.

topics.title: Agriculture: food security, markets and resource trade-offs
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory sector breadth: connect nutrition, price discovery and farm incentives. Deepen scheme eligibility from official current sources; avoid memorising every old subsidy rate.

nodes.label: Agriculture: food security, markets and resource trade-offs
Food security: quantity AND nutrition
APMC reform: market access and fair price discovery
e-NAM: connect markets and reduce information gaps
Input support can create resource and fiscal trade-offs

cells: Food availability
Food quantity and dietary quality are separate checks.
Aggregate grain availability alone does not establish adequate nutrition.
Regulated agricultural markets
Intended protections include fair prices and prompt payments.
A protective purpose does not rule out trader concentration or weak competition.
e-NAM
Electronic market information and trading link existing markets.
A portal alone does not prove all farmers can realise better prices.
Power and price support
Support changes input costs and production incentives.
Consider groundwater use, fiscal cost and uneven crop/region access.

cards.question: Illustrative case: grain stocks rise but child nutrition remains weak. What distinction matters?
cards.answer: Availability is only the quantitative dimension. Examine diet quality, access and the delivery of nutritional support before concluding that food security has improved.

cards.question: Build a descriptive outline on agricultural market reform.
cards.answer: Define the marketing problem; explain information/competition barriers; discuss market-linking interventions; evaluate access, implementation and producer outcomes; conclude with safeguards. Do not list portals without mechanisms.

cards.question: Why can a farm-support measure have both benefits and costs?
cards.answer: Support can reduce risk or costs but alter resource use and distribution. Analyse the particular subsidy rather than asserting that all support is good or bad.

cards.question: What is enough depth for this sector packet?
cards.answer: Explain food security, market reform and one support trade-off closed-book, then practise a scheme eligibility case using current verified rules. Skip crop encyclopaedias and stale numeric limits; retain syllabus breadth.

topics.title: Industry: reforms, approvals and productive capacity
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Study the reform-to-investment channel, not an inventory of launch dates. Distinguish fewer barriers, easier approvals and actual productive investment.

nodes.label: Industry: reforms, approvals and productive capacity
1991 policy: shift from regulatory control toward development
Delicensing: greater entry and expansion freedom
Disinvestment: changes government ownership
Single-window approvals and land information

cells: Delicensing
Reduces prior industrial-permission requirements.
Does not mean every industry is exempt from all law.
Disinvestment
Reduces the government's equity stake.
A change in stake alone is not proof of better productivity.
National Single Window System
Helps identify and apply for relevant approvals.
The source describes guidance: identifying an approval is not automatically granting it.
Industrial Land Bank
Provides information for comparing industrial sites.
Information access does not eliminate infrastructure or execution constraints.

cards.question: Illustrative case: approvals become easier but a plant is not built. Is reform necessarily ineffective?
cards.answer: Separate the intended reduction in permission friction from investment outcomes. Identify other constraints and evaluate actual investment, productivity and jobs rather than portal activity alone.

cards.question: Compare delicensing and disinvestment.
cards.answer: Delicensing concerns entry/expansion permission; disinvestment concerns government equity. They are distinct reform instruments with different transmission channels.

cards.question: Plan a 400-word answer on industrial reform.
cards.answer: Define the constraint; select reform instruments; trace incentives into investment/productivity; assess implementation and inclusion; conclude. Use a few verified current anchors, not every historical policy date.

cards.question: Depth checkpoint: what should be retrieved?
cards.answer: Explain two reform mechanisms and two distinct approval/site-information tools. Add a limitation to each. Current institutional counts in the notes are not permanent facts.

topics.title: Services: output, jobs, insurance and logistics
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Cover services through common dimensions: output, employment, productivity, exports and access. Use definitions accurately; update reported sector shares before exam use.

nodes.label: Services: output, jobs, insurance and logistics
GDP share, employment and productivity are different indicators
Insurance penetration: premiums relative to GDP
Insurance density: premiums per person
Logistics policy: coordination and cost competitiveness

cells: Output share
Measures a sector's contribution to output.
A large output share does not by itself establish an equally large employment share.
Labour productivity
Output per unit of labour input.
Specify persons or hours and compare like periods.
Insurance penetration versus density
Premium/GDP versus premium/population.
The denominators and units differ; neither alone measures claim quality or protection adequacy.
Logistics policy
Aims to improve costs, coordination and data-driven decisions.
Targets are not achieved outcomes.

cards.question: Original practice: premiums are 40 units, GDP is 1,000 units and population is 20. Calculate penetration and density.
cards.answer: Penetration = 40/1,000 x 100 = 4%. Density = 40/20 = 2 currency units per person. These inputs are invented to test the denominators.

cards.question: Does fast services growth guarantee enough jobs for all skill groups?
cards.answer: No. Compare employment with output and examine skill requirements/productivity. The two shares cannot be substituted for each other.

cards.question: Build a services-led development answer outline.
cards.answer: Describe output/jobs/export channels; distinguish subsectors; explain productivity and access constraints; evaluate logistics/digital support; conclude on broad employment quality. Do not treat all services as equally skill-intensive.

cards.question: How much sector trivia should be retained?
cards.answer: Learn the indicator distinctions and two subsector mechanisms deeply. Use dated verified numbers only when they support an argument; do not memorise every projected market size.

topics.title: External sector: trade, capital flows and convertibility
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Explain how trade, financial flows and policy interact. Keep BoP accounting separate from claims about development; the source itself gives inconsistent convertibility dates, preserved for review.

nodes.label: External sector: trade, capital flows and convertibility
Trade opening: imports, exports and competitiveness
BoP: transactions with the rest of the world over a period
FDI versus portfolio investment
Current-account versus capital-account convertibility

cells: Balance of payments
Records cross-border goods, services, transfers and investment transactions.
It is a period-based transaction record, not just merchandise exports minus imports.
FDI
Investment associated with a lasting business/control relationship.
Do not infer the legal threshold from the label alone; verify current applicable rules.
Portfolio investment
Investment in financial assets such as traded securities.
Not the same ownership/control relationship as a direct-investment example.
Convertibility
Current transactions and capital/asset transactions have distinct rules.
The notes disagree on the current-account convertibility year; do not memorise either without verification.

cards.question: Illustrative classification: buying goods abroad versus buying a foreign financial asset.
cards.answer: The goods purchase is a current-transaction example; the financial-asset purchase involves a capital/financial transaction. Applicable permissions still need checking.

cards.question: Can a services surplus matter even if merchandise trade is in deficit?
cards.answer: Yes. The notes explain that invisibles/services earnings and remittances can offset some goods-trade deficit. Inspect the complete accounts instead of equating the merchandise balance with the entire BoP.

cards.question: Outline an answer on opening the external sector.
cards.answer: Define the opening; explain trade and capital-flow channels; discuss competitiveness and financing; evaluate vulnerability and policy safeguards; conclude with a balanced judgement. Omit unsupported claims that all trade deficits are bad.

cards.question: Which source ambiguity needs resolving first?
cards.answer: Page 6 says current-account convertibility since 1994; page 19 states an August 1993 date. These are incompatible source observations of the stated milestone, not two confirmed historical facts.

facts.label: Year of India's current-account convertibility milestone (source inconsistency)

observations.as_of: Undated notes, PDF page 6; historical milestone claim
Undated notes, PDF page 19; historical milestone claim

topics.title: International institutions: mandate, finance and reports
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory globalisation breadth plus objective report knowledge. Match institutions to functions and reports; do not memorise mutable membership counts from undated notes.

nodes.label: International institutions: mandate, finance and reports
IMF: quotas, governance and capacity development
IBRD and IDA together form the World Bank
IFC: private-sector development financing
WTO: rules for goods, services and intellectual property

cells: IMF governance
Quota-based voting and member representation.
A quota share is not an equal one-country-one-vote arrangement.
IBRD versus IDA
Development finance versus concessional support for poorer countries.
World Bank and the wider World Bank Group are not identical labels.
IFC
Financing oriented to private-sector development.
Do not attribute every World Bank Group activity to IBRD.
WTO versus GATT
The notes contrast WTO's institutional structure and wider subject coverage.
Do not reduce WTO solely to merchandise tariffs.

cards.question: Which two institutions are jointly called the World Bank?
cards.answer: IBRD and IDA. The World Bank Group is broader; distinguish IFC and the other arms rather than treating every name as interchangeable.

cards.question: Which report fields should be retrieved beyond a publisher name?
cards.answer: Publisher, edition/reference period, framework/measure, findings and India implications. The notes identify World Bank reports such as World Development Report and Global Economic Prospects; the monthly forecast packet supplies a dated illustration.

cards.question: Build a comparison-based globalisation answer.
cards.answer: Choose a function or problem first, then compare institutional mandates, financing/rules and practical limitations. Avoid a disconnected list of headquarters and presidents.

cards.question: What should be updated rather than learned as permanent?
cards.answer: Membership, quota shares, leadership, eligibility thresholds and latest report findings. Keep the stable mandate map; verify mutable values against official releases.

topics.title: Economic thought: assumptions, demand and policy response
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Selective theory support: compare classical adjustment and Keynesian demand management intuitively. Do not let advanced diagrams displace higher-priority ESI issues.

nodes.label: Economic thought: assumptions, demand and policy response
Classical presentation: flexible wages/prices and long-run adjustment
Keynesian presentation: short-run constraints
Insufficient demand can restrain output and employment
Public spending can support demand in a depressed economy

cells: Time horizon
Classical discussion stresses long-run adjustment; Keynesian discussion stresses short-run conditions.
Do not compare conclusions without comparing assumptions.
Wage/price adjustment
Flexibility supports a self-adjusting account.
Rigidities change the speed and outcome of adjustment.
Demand shortfall
Spending can restrain output when productive capacity is unused.
Do not assume the same response when capacity and supply are binding.
Government role
Laissez-faire versus active demand support in the stylised comparison.
These are learning models, not universal policy slogans.

cards.question: Illustrative case: unused capacity and falling demand. What channel could public expenditure support?
cards.answer: Aggregate spending can support output and employment when demand is deficient. State the unused-capacity assumption and discuss limits; do not promise a costless outcome.

cards.question: Why are model assumptions examinable?
cards.answer: Changing the time horizon, adjustment speed or capacity assumptions can change the conclusion. Explain the mechanism instead of memorising that one school is always correct.

cards.question: Stopping rule for this chapter?
cards.answer: Retrieve the common comparison dimensions and apply one demand-shock case. Return to this reference only when a policy question reveals a gap; advanced derivations are lower priority.

topics.title: Planning: objectives, instruments and institutional transition
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Selective historical breadth: remember the purpose and broad strategy shifts. Use the readable short notes; the full planning PDF has no extractable text and is catalogued as reference only.

nodes.label: Planning: objectives, instruments and institutional transition
Planning matches policy instruments to long-term objectives
Imperative versus indicative planning
Growth/jobs and distribution are distinct objectives
Planning Commission to NITI Aayog: institutional transition

cells: Imperative planning
Directive allocation with a central authority.
Do not confuse it with all forms of government coordination.
Indicative planning
Government facilitates and influences private decisions.
A facilitator still shapes incentives and policy priorities.
Economic versus social objectives
Output/employment alongside distribution and justice.
A higher aggregate income does not automatically settle distribution.
Mahalanobis strategy
Emphasis on heavy/capital-goods industrial capacity and self-reliance.
The notes also describe foreign-exchange constraints: evaluate feasibility.

cards.question: Compare plan targets with outcomes: what is the basic trap?
cards.answer: A stated target is not an achieved outcome. Explain strategy and constraints rather than reproducing every target-growth table.

cards.question: Outline a short answer on planning institutions.
cards.answer: Explain planning purpose; distinguish planning types; trace broad institutional change; assess coordination and implementation. Treat plan-era budget classifications in old notes as historical, not automatically current.

cards.question: What should be prioritised over all twelve plan dates?
cards.answer: A few strategy transitions, growth-versus-distribution objectives, and the Commission-to-NITI transition. Use detailed chronology as reference for targeted gaps.

topics.title: Before Independence: structural constraints and development
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Selective context for explaining reform needs: agricultural stagnation, structural dependence and the difference between demographic potential and realised development.

nodes.label: Before Independence: structural constraints and development
Agriculture: livelihood dependence with weak productivity
Cash-crop orientation and colonial trade incentives
Industrial deterioration constrained diversification
Demographic dividend is potential, not an automatic benefit

cells: Livelihood dependence
A large agricultural dependence can coexist with poor productivity.
Dependence is not a measure of agricultural prosperity.
Cash crops
Production incentives can shift toward export-oriented crops.
Production volume alone does not establish household food access.
Diversification
Weak industrial opportunities limit structural transformation.
Do not infer modern sector shares from colonial observations.
Demographic dividend
A working-age structure creates economic potential.
Jobs and human capabilities are needed to realise the opportunity.

cards.question: How can colonial context support an answer without overwhelming it?
cards.answer: Use one relevant structural constraint to explain why an intervention was pursued, then analyse its mechanism and outcome. Avoid an entire historical narrative in a current-policy answer.

cards.question: Does a working-age population automatically create a dividend?
cards.answer: No. The notes define economic potential from age structure; an answer still needs employment and capability channels.

cards.question: What is enough preparation depth?
cards.answer: Explain two structural constraints and one reform motivation. Keep historical numerical series in reference unless explicitly demanded.

topics.title: 1947-1991: compare sector strategies and their constraints
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: A compact comparison across the historical macro, agriculture, industry, services and external-sector folders. These selected pages are context, not an exhaustive historical synthesis.

nodes.label: 1947-1991: compare sector strategies and their constraints
Macro: planned development from structural underdevelopment
Agriculture: land reform and an input/credit package
Industry: capital-goods strategy and rural demand linkages
Services: productivity and employment need separate checks
External policy: import substitution and self-reliance

cells: Macro strategy
Planning sought growth from a weak structural starting point.
Targets, actual outcomes and shocks must be distinguished.
Land reform and Green Revolution inputs
Tenure/ownership measures differ from technology, water and credit support.
Unequal access can distribute gains unevenly.
Heavy industry
Capital-goods capacity formed a strategic priority.
Agricultural/rural-income weakness can reduce industrial demand.
Services
High productivity is not identical to broad employment absorption.
This history-labelled source includes later structural observations; do not assume every page describes only 1947-91.
Import substitution
Protection aimed to reduce external dependence and build domestic capability.
Assess costs and competitiveness as well as the intended objective.

cards.question: Illustrative mechanism: a farm-output shock affects a factory. Explain.
cards.answer: Lower agricultural output can reduce rural incomes and demand for industrial goods, while agro-based industries can also face input shortages. Distinguish demand and input channels.

cards.question: Compare agricultural land reform with an input package.
cards.answer: Land reform addresses ownership/tenure/incentives; input packages address technology and production resources. They address different constraints and can interact.

cards.question: Build a 1991-transition answer without listing every policy date.
cards.answer: Start with inherited constraints; contrast pre-reform sector strategies with opening/competition; evaluate intended channels and distribution; conclude using relevant evidence rather than chronology.

cards.question: What is the stopping rule for historical sector notes?
cards.answer: Retrieve one intervention, one mechanism and one limitation per sector. Deepen historical detail only when an actual practice demand reveals a gap.

topics.title: ESI glossary: retrieve a concept, then apply it
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: A small concept-use packet drawn from selected dictionary entries. All eight dictionary PDFs remain searchable in the catalogue; they are references, not eight books to memorise.

nodes.label: ESI glossary: retrieve a concept, then apply it
BoP: cross-border transaction record over a period
Crowding out: public activity may displace private spending
Externalities: effects on welfare beyond the transaction
Opportunity cost: the forgone alternative
Fiscal drag: rising tax burdens can restrain demand

cells: BoP
Account of transactions between residents and the rest of the world.
Not only merchandise trade.
Crowding out
A possible reduction of private spending associated with public expansion.
State the financing and capacity context; do not claim every public project crowds out.
Externality
A positive or negative effect beyond the immediate transaction.
Private output value and social welfare effects can differ.
Opportunity cost
The alternative forgone by committing scarce resources.
It need not be a separate cash payment.
Fiscal drag
Progressive tax effects can restrain demand as incomes move into higher brackets.
Distinguish a built-in effect from a new discretionary tax decision.

cards.question: Original case: a government spends scarce funds on project A instead of feasible project B. What is the concept?
cards.answer: Opportunity cost: the forgone alternative use of resources. Explain the alternative, not just the money paid for A.

cards.question: Original case: factory output rises but neighbouring households face pollution. What should the GDP discussion include?
cards.answer: A negative external effect on welfare. Analyse output and social costs separately; do not assume higher production measures every welfare consequence.

cards.question: How should the dictionary be used during mock-test repair?
cards.answer: Identify the missed concept; retrieve its definition; create an original example and counterexample; retest in a fresh question. Do not replace applied study with alphabetical memorisation.

topics.title: Growth and development: output, distribution and transformation
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: distinguish real output expansion from inclusive development; explain productivity and structural change, then test jobs, capabilities and environmental costs rather than dumping GDP figures.

nodes.label: Growth: sustained expansion of output
Investment, labour use and technology
Structural change in production and work
Development: broader quality of life
Poverty, inequality and employment outcomes
Pollution and resource depletion costs

cells: Output vs welfare
Growth tracks production; development also tests how people live.
Pair output evidence with health, education, work and poverty outcomes.
Capital vs technology
More equipment expands inputs; innovation can raise output from given resources.
Ask whether investment is productive, not simply large.
Sectoral shift vs inclusion
Moving away from agriculture changes economic structure.
Judge whether workers gain productive opportunities rather than assuming every shift improves welfare.
Trickle-down vs deliberate inclusion
The traditional approach assumes output gains spread; the modern approach tests broader outcomes.
Explain the missing transmission channel when poverty persists.
Private gains vs social costs
Output may rise alongside pollution and resource loss.
Include environmental costs before calling a project developmental.

cards.question: Illustrative calculation: real output rises from 400 to 424 units. What is growth?
cards.answer: (424 - 400) / 400 × 100 = 6%. These invented real-output units avoid confusing price increases with additional production; this is not an observed GDP estimate.

cards.question: Illustrative case: a factory raises output but nearby water becomes unsafe. Has development necessarily improved?
cards.answer: No. Separate the output gain from health, distribution and environmental effects. Examine who gains jobs, who bears the damage and whether prevention or compensation changes the net welfare assessment.

cards.question: Why can better technology matter without proportionately more capital?
cards.answer: It can improve how existing resources are used, increasing potential output. Capital quantity alone is therefore an incomplete explanation of productivity.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Growth is necessary but not a sufficient development strategy.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: define output versus well-being → explain investment/productivity and resource creation → trace jobs and public-service channels → identify inequality and pollution leakages → propose inclusive, environmentally responsible transmission → conclude with an outcome dashboard. Avoid presenting a disputed absolute necessity claim as a theorem.

cards.question: What depth should this chapter reach, and what should not dominate revision?
cards.answer: Master the growth/development distinction, two productivity mechanisms, one distribution channel and one environmental trade-off; practise a calculation and a balanced answer. Do not spend most revision time memorising long alternative-index lists, changing income cut-offs or undated ranks.

cards.question: How do the short notes triangulate the central distinction?
cards.answer: They also separate GDP-centred progress from wider inclusion and sustainability. Use this as a consistency check, not as evidence that all output gains automatically trickle down.

topics.title: Human development: capabilities, human capital and feedback
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: explain real freedoms as the end of development, human capital as a productive means, the growth–capability feedback loop and why average index gains can hide exclusion.

nodes.label: Human development: expand real choices
Capabilities: opportunities to do and be
Human capital: embodied skills and health
Education, health, training and information
Productive, adaptable workforce
Growth finances opportunities and services

cells: Human development
Asks whether people have meaningful opportunities.
Value health and education even beyond their contribution to output.
Human capital
Treats skills, knowledge and health as productive assets.
Trace how training improves productivity; do not reduce people only to inputs.
Capital formation
Education, health, training, migration and information require investment.
Distinguish the accumulation process from the stock of capacities.
Two-way relationship
Growth can fund services; capabilities can support growth.
Identify a failure on either side rather than assume automatic feedback.
Choice vs income alone
More money is an enabling resource, not a complete description of opportunity.
Ask whether a person can actually access learning, health and valued work.

cards.question: Distinguish a capability from a productive human-capital investment.
cards.answer: A capability concerns a person's real opportunity to live in a valued way. A training investment builds skills that can raise production. The same education may serve both purposes, but the evaluative lenses differ.

cards.question: Illustrative case: higher family income coexists with a girl being unable to attend school. What is missing?
cards.answer: Income alone does not establish a real educational choice. Diagnose barriers to using resources, then assess whether access to education and agency actually improve; do not equate purchasing power with achieved freedom.

cards.question: HDI and IHDI improve different parts of a development diagnosis. How?
cards.answer: HDI summarises average achievement in health, education and living standards. IHDI adds the distributional lens; an average can look good while opportunities remain uneven. This comparison does not require memorising current ranks.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Human development is both a means and an end.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: define capabilities → explain intrinsic value of health/education → show investment-to-productivity channel → show growth-to-services channel → identify exclusion that breaks the loop → recommend access, quality and distribution checks.

cards.question: What depth should human-development revision reach?
cards.answer: Explain the capability/human-capital distinction, reproduce the two-way loop and apply it to a health or education case. Learn index purpose and inequality caveats; do not over-study ranks, launch-year trivia or elaborate index arithmetic without verified methodology.

cards.question: Why include information alongside education and health?
cards.answer: People need information about learning institutions and jobs to make useful choices. The short notes treat expenditure on obtaining that information as human-capital formation; information complements rather than replaces access to services.

topics.title: Sustainability: resource limits, policy and intergenerational equity
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: connect present needs with future resource availability, explain growth–environment mechanisms, evaluate policy instruments and SDG implementation without treating an income threshold as automatic environmental repair.

nodes.label: Sustainability: present and future resource use
Renewables: use must respect regeneration
Production can damage environmental quality
Standards, efficient technology and public transport
Intergenerational equity and prudent depletion
SDGs: integrated objectives and implementation

cells: Renewable vs exhaustible
Renewables regenerate; exhaustible resources require prudent depletion.
Renewable does not mean unlimited: compare extraction with replenishment.
Efficiency vs conservation
Efficient techniques reduce resource needs; conservation also protects future availability.
Check resource pressure, not technology adoption alone.
EKC vs policy guarantee
The inverted-U is a theoretical relationship, not an assured path.
Technology, regulation and governance determine whether pollution falls.
Standards vs public investment
Emission limits constrain behaviour; public transport provides an alternative.
Combine enforcement with feasible ways to comply.
SDG agenda vs monitoring
SDGs specify linked goals; the SDG India Index supports subnational comparison.
Use monitoring to identify implementation gaps, not just celebrate rankings.

cards.question: Illustrative resource case: a forest regenerates 8 units annually and harvest is 11. What is the warning?
cards.answer: Harvest exceeds regeneration by 3 invented units per year, signalling depletion pressure. A sustainable plan must respect regeneration and future usefulness; the arithmetic is illustrative, not a forestry estimate.

cards.question: Why is 'grow first, clean up automatically later' a weak argument?
cards.answer: The EKC describes a possible non-linear pattern. Its cleaner phase depends on technology, regulation, awareness and other conditions; income alone is not a policy instrument.

cards.question: Illustrative case: a vehicle emission rule fails because workers lack alternatives. What complementary policy fits?
cards.answer: Improve usable public transport while enforcing standards. Explain the mechanism: a practical travel alternative can reduce dependence on private vehicles rather than placing all adjustment costs on commuters.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Reconcile development and environmental protection.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: define present/future needs → identify output and livelihood benefits → trace pollution and depletion costs → match standards, technology and transport to causes → discuss who bears adjustment costs → monitor social and environmental outcomes through the SDG framework.

cards.question: What depth is appropriate, and what should not be over-studied?
cards.answer: Know regeneration versus depletion, intergenerational equity, the conditional EKC, a policy mix and the role of SDG monitoring. Do not memorise every target or recycle old climate pledges as achieved outcomes; avoid assuming all natural assets are replaceable by machines.

cards.question: What useful cross-check do the short notes provide?
cards.answer: They restate the regeneration limit, equitable use across generations, public transport and emission controls. Use the full notes' explicit EKC caveat to qualify the short version's compressed description.

topics.title: Poverty: incidence, depth, capabilities and vulnerability
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: distinguish absolute, relative and multidimensional poverty; interpret incidence versus shortfall, trace poverty traps and match persistent deprivation or temporary shocks to suitable policy responses.

nodes.label: Poverty: inadequate resources and opportunities
Absolute and relative poverty lenses
Incidence, shortfall and severity
Multidimensional deprivation
Chronic, churning and occasional poverty
Weak work and unequal assets constrain mobility

cells: Absolute vs relative
A minimum threshold differs from disadvantage relative to others.
State the benchmark before comparing poverty across societies.
Incidence vs depth
Headcount asks how many are poor; a gap asks how far below the line they are.
A policy may reduce shortfalls before anyone crosses the line.
Depth vs severity
Squared gaps give more weight to larger shortfalls.
Do not infer identical hardship from identical headcount ratios.
Chronic vs transient
Persistent deprivation differs from repeated entry or an occasional shock.
Combine durable livelihood/asset support with appropriate shock protection.
Monetary vs multidimensional
Consumption or income cannot fully capture health, learning and living conditions.
Use the two lenses together; do not treat different indices as interchangeable.

cards.question: Illustrative calculation: 24 of 120 people are below a defined poverty line. What is the headcount ratio?
cards.answer: HCR = 24/120 × 100 = 20%. It says nothing about each poor person's shortfall. These are invented people and a hypothetical threshold, not a poverty estimate.

cards.question: Illustrative shortfall: line 100 units; one person's consumption 70. What can and cannot be concluded?
cards.answer: The person's normalised gap is (100 - 70)/100 = 30%. This is an individual shortfall example, not the population poverty-gap index. One observation cannot establish an area's average gap or severity.

cards.question: Why might poverty headcount stay unchanged after a useful transfer?
cards.answer: An illustrative transfer can raise a poor household's resources while leaving it below the line. Depth may improve without an immediate change in incidence; assess both rather than conclude the transfer had no effect.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Poverty reduction needs more than growth.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: define monetary and capability deprivation → describe low-quality work and unequal asset access → distinguish chronic from shock-driven poverty → match livelihoods, services and protection to those causes → discuss targeting and durable mobility → evaluate incidence, depth and multiple deprivations.

cards.question: What poverty depth is essential, and what should not consume revision?
cards.answer: Be fluent in absolute/relative, incidence/depth/severity, multidimensionality and chronic/transient distinctions; practise one calculation and one mechanism-led policy answer. Learn estimation history selectively, not a dump of old rupee thresholds, calorie norms or incomparable PPP lines.

cards.question: Illustrative case: income rises but unsafe water and missed schooling persist. Has every poverty dimension disappeared?
cards.answer: No. The monetary improvement and non-monetary deprivations may coexist. Diagnose which service or opportunity gaps remain; do not assert an MPI classification without its specified indicators and cut-offs.

topics.title: Demography: population change, dependency and the dividend
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: separate natural increase from migration, interpret crude rates and age composition, and explain why a demographic opportunity produces growth only with health, skills, participation and productive jobs.

nodes.label: Population: births, deaths and migration
Mortality and fertility change at different speeds
Age composition and dependency
Working-age potential, not automatic growth
Health, education, skills and job creation
Ageing changes care and work needs

edges.label: can create a favourable work-age balance
also requires planning for later-life needs

cells: CBR vs CDR
Births and deaths each use mid-year population, usually per thousand.
Age composition can distort cross-population comparisons of crude death rates.
Natural vs actual growth
Natural increase excludes migration; actual change includes net migration.
Do not infer fertility change from total population change alone.
Transition vs fixed stages
Mortality decline may precede fertility decline, temporarily widening the gap.
Explain the mechanism rather than treating disputed stage numbering as universal.
Dependency vs unemployment
Age dependency is a demographic relationship, not a count of actual joblessness.
A working-age person is not necessarily a worker.
Dividend vs ageing
A favourable age mix creates opportunity; later ageing creates different needs.
Invest in capabilities and jobs now while planning health and support needs.

cards.question: Illustrative calculation: births 900, deaths 400, in-migrants 250, out-migrants 100. What changes?
cards.answer: Natural increase = 900 - 400 = 500 people. Actual increase = 500 + 250 - 100 = 650. With an illustrative mid-year population of 50,000, CBR = 18 and CDR = 8 per thousand; natural increase is 10 per thousand. These are invented counts.

cards.question: Why can a healthier, older population show a higher crude death rate?
cards.answer: Crude rates use the whole population without adjusting for age. More older people can raise the crude death rate even when survival conditions are better; examine age composition before ranking health systems.

cards.question: Illustrative case: the working-age share grows but vacancies and skills lag. Is the dividend assured?
cards.answer: No. Demographic potential needs productive employment and capabilities. Skills deficits, poor health and jobless growth can prevent the age structure from translating into higher output.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'The demographic dividend is conditional.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: define the age-composition opportunity → explain mortality/fertility sequence → trace participation, productivity and saving channels → identify skills, health and job constraints → propose capability and employment measures → note state differences and ageing → conclude with outcomes rather than a fixed national expiry date.

cards.question: What depth is needed, and what should not dominate?
cards.answer: Know population accounting, crude-rate units, dependency versus actual employment and the conditional dividend. Practise one calculation and a jobs–skills–health answer. Avoid memorising old projected shares, exact dividend-window dates, alleged ideal pyramids or inconsistent stage numbering.

cards.question: Illustrative case: two states have different age profiles. Why avoid one identical policy package?
cards.answer: The dividend's timing varies across states. A younger state may prioritise capability-building and job absorption; an older state also needs stronger ageing-related healthcare and appropriate work options. These are illustrative policy applications, not state rankings.

topics.title: Health: prevention, access and financial protection
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory syllabus breadth: explain health as well-being and a development input, distinguish prevention from treatment and financial protection from service availability, and prepare one coherent delivery-reform answer.

nodes.label: Health: well-being, not only absence of illness
Public health: prevention and collective action
Access: staff, facilities and affordable medicines
Financing: protect households from medical costs
Health supports attendance and productive days
Coordination, quality and accountability

cells: Well-being vs disease absence
Health includes physical, mental and social dimensions.
Assess functioning and quality of life, not treatment counts alone.
Prevention vs cure
Public-health action lowers disease risks; treatment responds to illness.
Use nutrition, hygiene and preventive care alongside clinical services.
Coverage vs availability
Financial coverage does not itself create clinicians, medicines or facilities.
Check both payment barriers and local service capacity.
Public vs private provision
Both sectors deliver care, with different roles and access conditions.
Evaluate affordability and quality rather than assume ownership alone ensures performance.
Health vs economic feedback
Illness reduces productivity; prevention can release resources.
Connect healthier children and workers to learning and output, without inventing benefit ratios.

cards.question: Illustrative case: a family has financial coverage but no nearby qualified provider. What remains unsolved?
cards.answer: Supply-side access remains weak. Financial protection must be complemented by personnel, facilities, medicines and accountable quality; coverage on paper is not the same as usable care.

cards.question: How can preventive health support education and the economy?
cards.answer: Better health can reduce absence and production losses, help children attend school and reduce avoidable treatment spending. Explain the chain rather than attach an unsupported numerical multiplier.

cards.question: Illustrative case: a hospital expands but unsafe water and poor nutrition persist. Why is that incomplete?
cards.answer: Treatment capacity addresses only part of the burden. Nutrition, hygiene and preventive medicine influence illness before patients reach a hospital; a development strategy needs both determinants and care.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Improve health outcomes without equating reform to more insurance alone.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: define broad well-being → identify prevention and social determinants → map personnel/infrastructure/medicine barriers → pair financial protection with primary service capacity → address quality and coordination → evaluate access, household burden and health outcomes.

cards.question: What is mandatory breadth, and what should not be over-studied?
cards.answer: Prepare prevention versus cure, supply versus financing, one growth linkage and a balanced delivery answer. This is mandatory coverage, not a skip topic. Do not memorise every committee, old mortality series or scheme benefit limit without current verification.

cards.question: Why is medical spending alone not a sufficient performance measure?
cards.answer: Resources matter, but staffing, governance, affordability and medicine access determine whether they produce usable, safe care. Link inputs to access and outcomes instead of assuming expenditure automatically creates health.

topics.title: Education: access, learning and equitable opportunity
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory syllabus breadth: distinguish forms of learning, enrolment and meaningful educational opportunity; explain access–quality–equity and prepare a reform answer that separates policy aspirations from achieved results.

nodes.label: Education: learning and capability-building
Formal, non-formal and informal learning
Access, affordability and continuation
Quality and competency-oriented learning
Rights and inclusion of disadvantaged learners
Occupational opportunity and social participation

edges.label: must be paired with useful learning

cells: Formal vs non-formal
Institutional schooling differs from organised learning outside that system.
Use complementary routes for groups excluded from regular provision.
Informal vs organised
Daily experience can teach without a structured programme.
Do not call every non-school activity non-formal education.
Enrolment vs learning
GER measures participation, not mastery of competencies.
Pair access with retention and learning checks.
Right vs delivery
A legal commitment to education still requires usable provision.
Ask whether disadvantaged learners can attend and continue.
Reform target vs achievement
NEP describes policy direction and planned changes.
Do not write a target as if implementation and results are already complete.

cards.question: Illustrative GER calculation: total enrolment is 1,080 and official age-group population is 1,000. Is 108% impossible?
cards.answer: GER = 1,080/1,000 × 100 = 108%. It includes enrolled learners irrespective of age, so it need not be bounded at 100%. It does not show that every age-eligible child is enrolled or learning. These are invented counts.

cards.question: Illustrative case: a school enrols more children but skills remain weak. Which distinction matters?
cards.answer: Access has expanded, but enrolment is not equivalent to learning quality. Diagnose teaching and competency outcomes alongside continuation and equitable participation, rather than dismissing either access or quality.

cards.question: Classify an organised evening course for migrant workers versus a child learning from everyday family experience.
cards.answer: The structured course outside regular institutions is an illustrative non-formal route. Learning through daily experience without organised instruction is informal. Neither is automatically a substitute for adequate formal provision.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Make education expansion inclusive and meaningful.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: define access and learning → distinguish participation from competencies → identify affordability and inclusion barriers → connect rights with delivery → discuss quality, flexible learning and continuation → treat reform proposals as proposals → evaluate access, retention and learning together.

cards.question: What is mandatory breadth, and what should not dominate revision?
cards.answer: Know the three learning forms, enrolment versus learning, the role of educational rights and access–equity–quality. Prepare one GER example and a reform skeleton. Do not skip the topic, but avoid long committee histories, undated counts and claims that every NEP aspiration is implemented.

cards.question: Why is education also an ESI development issue rather than only a school-system issue?
cards.answer: Learning influences productivity, occupational opportunities, inequality and social participation. A useful answer connects those mechanisms with who gains access to good education, instead of listing programmes alone.

topics.title: Gender: agency, resources, care and participation
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: use health, education, work and representation as distinct lenses; explain how norms, unpaid care and asset control shape agency, then evaluate an equity-oriented policy mix without relying on one headline ratio.

nodes.label: Gender inequality: unequal opportunities and agency
Norms, stereotypes and unequal care roles
Access to and control over assets
Participation, employment and remuneration
Health and educational opportunities
Decision-making and political participation

edges.label: tests substantive agency, not presence alone
income matters more when control improves

cells: Sex ratio vs agency
Population composition is not equivalent to control over life choices.
Read demographic indicators alongside work, assets and decision-making.
LFPR vs WPR
Labour-force membership includes work-seeking/availability; WPR counts employment.
Use the same population group and look at job access, not participation alone.
Formal rights vs lived control
Legal recognition can coexist with unequal practical access to property.
Ask who owns, uses and makes decisions over resources.
Equality vs equity
A common entitlement differs from support responsive to unequal starting conditions.
An equitable design tackles barriers without treating women as a uniform group.
Representation vs substantive voice
Seats or presence do not alone establish equal power.
Assess meaningful decision-making alongside the representation measure.

cards.question: Illustrative case: women complete education but cannot accept distant jobs because care responsibilities are unequal. What is the mechanism?
cards.answer: Capabilities do not automatically become employment. Unequal care roles and restrictive norms constrain usable job choices; an illustrative response combines safe access to work, care support and fair opportunities rather than education alone.

cards.question: Illustrative calculation: 30,000 female births and 32,000 male births. What is sex ratio at birth in the Indian convention?
cards.answer: 30,000/32,000 × 1,000 = 937.5 girls per 1,000 boys. State the convention and reference population. This invented example is not the overall population sex ratio and cannot establish women's agency.

cards.question: Distinguish maternal morbidity from maternal mortality ratio.
cards.answer: Morbidity concerns pregnancy/childbirth-related illness or disability; the mortality ratio counts maternal deaths relative to live births. Do not interchange health burden with death counts or quote an undated current value.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Women's empowerment is more than numerical representation.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: define agency → organise evidence across health, education, work, assets and voice → trace norms and care constraints → distinguish formal rights from lived control → propose capability, access and decision-making measures → discuss unequal starting conditions → assess substantive outcomes.

cards.question: What gender depth is essential, and what must not be over-studied?
cards.answer: Master indicator distinctions, care/norms-to-work mechanisms, asset control, equality versus equity and a multi-domain answer. Avoid undated ranks or productivity percentages; verify law commencement and current legal text separately because these notes contain contradictory legal claims.

cards.question: Illustrative case: a property title includes a woman but she cannot decide its use. Is empowerment complete?
cards.answer: No. Formal recognition differs from practical control. Ask whether she can make decisions, benefit from the asset and exercise voice; a document alone does not resolve bargaining inequalities.

topics.title: Positive discrimination: substantive equality and representation
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory syllabus breadth: explain why identical treatment can preserve historical disadvantage, distinguish reservation from wider inclusion and evaluate representation, targeting and complementary capability support without asserting unverified legal details.

nodes.label: Affirmative action: address historical disadvantage
Substantive equality and social mobility
Reservation across education, jobs and representation
Voice and access for disadvantaged groups
Targeting and distribution within eligible groups
Implementation concerns, stigma and fairness debates

cells: Formal vs substantive equality
An identical rule need not remove accumulated disadvantage.
Explain historical exclusion and access barriers before judging differential support.
Reservation vs overall inclusion
Reserved opportunities are one institutional tool, not the entire equality agenda.
Assess actual advancement and mobility, not seat allocation alone.
Education vs jobs
Access to learning and public employment concern different entry points.
Do not assume the same eligibility and implementation rules apply everywhere.
Representation vs advancement
A political voice channel differs from the broader educational/economic objective.
Connect participation to substantive opportunities and outcomes.
Group eligibility vs benefit capture
A disadvantaged group can contain more advanced members.
Discuss targeting carefully; verify category-specific rules rather than assert one universal income test.

cards.question: Why might formally identical treatment fail to create equal opportunity?
cards.answer: Past exclusion can leave unequal resources and institutional access. An affirmative measure seeks to change those starting conditions; evaluate whether it improves representation and mobility rather than assume different treatment is inherently unfair or automatically sufficient.

cards.question: Illustrative case: reserved educational access expands, but entrants lack academic support. How should the response be framed?
cards.answer: Treat access as a gain and identify the complementary capability gap. An illustrative policy package adds learning support and tracks completion and opportunity; this is an original application, not a claim about a particular institution.

cards.question: How should merit-related objections be handled in an analytical answer?
cards.answer: Acknowledge fairness and implementation concerns, then examine unequal prior opportunities, actual performance and mobility. Avoid treating beneficiaries as inherently less capable or treating every criticism as settled evidence against the policy.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Evaluate positive discrimination as an inclusion instrument.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: define the historical-disadvantage rationale → contrast formal/substantive equality → distinguish education, employment and representation tools → explain mobility benefits → examine targeting, stigma and implementation concerns → add capability support and transparent review → conclude using access and outcomes, not slogans.

cards.question: What is mandatory breadth, and what must not be over-studied?
cards.answer: Know rationale, tool distinctions, representation, targeting and a balanced answer. Do not skip the chapter. Avoid memorising every commission, numerical quota, creamy-layer ceiling or amendment timeline from these notes; verify precise legal provisions and effective dates separately.

cards.question: What does Article 46 add at a high level to this topic?
cards.answer: The notes connect it to promoting educational and economic interests of weaker sections. Use that broad advancement objective to explain why an inclusion strategy is wider than an isolated recruitment rule; do not infer a specific quota entitlement from this general direction.

topics.title: Multiculturalism: recognition, inclusion and common citizenship
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory syllabus breadth: distinguish the fact of cultural diversity from policies of accommodation, compare recognition with redistribution and balance group protection with individual rights and shared civic participation.

nodes.label: Multiculturalism: recognition and accommodation
Diversity: multiple cultures coexist
Recognition addresses identity-based exclusion
Accommodation and representation tools
Individual rights and shared civic interests
Participation through education, language and work

edges.label: poses a policy question, not an automatic answer
must be tested against individual freedom

cells: Diversity vs multiculturalism
Diversity describes coexistence; multiculturalism advocates recognition and accommodation.
A diverse city can still have exclusionary institutions.
Recognition vs redistribution
Identity-related disadvantage is not only a resource-allocation problem.
Consider both respectful treatment and material opportunities.
Assimilation vs accommodation
Absorption into majority norms differs from protecting cultural differences.
Enable participation without requiring cultural erasure.
Group rights vs individual rights
Protecting a community can sometimes restrict people within it.
Check internal freedom as well as majority–minority relations.
Symbolic celebration vs substantive inclusion
Public celebration may coexist with unequal education, jobs and voice.
Judge whether recognition changes real opportunities and participation.

cards.question: Illustrative case: a city holds a cultural festival but public services remain inaccessible in minority languages. What is the gap?
cards.answer: Symbolic celebration has not resolved substantive access. An illustrative response uses appropriate language access and participation mechanisms while assessing resources and shared civic needs; a festival alone is not inclusion.

cards.question: Why does redistribution alone not exhaust multicultural policy?
cards.answer: Disadvantage can involve disrespect, exclusion from representation and pressure to abandon an identity. Resource transfers may help material conditions without correcting those recognition problems.

cards.question: Illustrative case: a community invokes cultural protection to restrict members' choices. What should an answer test?
cards.answer: Test both protection against majority domination and the individual rights of people within the group. Cultural recognition does not automatically justify internal restrictions; explain the tension rather than rank cultures.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Diversity requires recognition and common citizenship.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: distinguish diversity from a policy stance → explain recognition and material inequality → compare accommodation with assimilation → discuss representation and service access → test group claims against individual rights and common interests → propose substantive participation → evaluate inclusion, not symbolism alone.

cards.question: What is mandatory breadth, and what should not be over-studied?
cards.answer: Prepare diversity/policy, recognition/redistribution and group/individual-right distinctions plus one balanced case. Do not skip it, but avoid memorising every labelled subtype or philosopher; do not reduce communities to fixed stereotypes.

cards.question: Can integration preserve distinct cultures?
cards.answer: Yes, in an accommodation-oriented approach, access to education, language learning, jobs and civic participation need not demand complete absorption into majority cultural practices. The policy test is meaningful participation with rights protection.

topics.title: Urbanisation and migration: drivers, agglomeration and inclusion
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: distinguish urban population growth from migration alone, explain push–pull drivers and agglomeration, assess origin/destination effects and match urban-service and inclusion policies to real constraints.

nodes.label: Urban change: population, classification and movement
Migration: varied motives and degrees of choice
Push–pull forces: livelihoods, services and safety
Density and connectivity can support productivity
Congestion, housing stress and environmental costs
Infrastructure, land-use planning and inclusion

edges.label: contributes, but is not the only component
requires service capacity to keep pace
can reduce planning and access failures

cells: Urbanisation vs urban growth
A rising urban share differs from the absolute addition of urban residents.
Check the population base and definition before comparing places.
Natural increase vs migration
Births minus deaths, net movement and reclassification all affect urban totals.
Do not attribute every new urban resident to rural out-migration.
Push vs pull
Origin hardships and destination attractions jointly shape movement.
Diagnose jobs, services, safety and environmental pressures at both ends.
Voluntary vs forced movement
Economic choice differs from displacement with little or no viable option.
Do not treat every migrant as a voluntary job seeker or every displaced person as a cross-border refugee.
Agglomeration vs congestion
Density/connectivity can support productivity; inadequate planning can raise costs.
Judge infrastructure, housing and inclusion rather than assume city growth is automatically developmental.

cards.question: Illustrative calculation: urban residents increase by 20,000; natural increase is 8,000 and reclassification adds 5,000. What is the residual net migration?
cards.answer: 20,000 - 8,000 - 5,000 = 7,000, assuming these exhaust the components and boundaries are consistently defined. These invented figures show why urban growth is not identical to migration.

cards.question: Illustrative case: workers move after crop failure toward a city with vacancies. Identify push and pull.
cards.answer: Crop failure and fragile livelihoods are origin-side pushes; jobs and income prospects are destination-side pulls. Both can act together, and movement may involve constrained choice rather than a simple preference.

cards.question: Why can migration help an origin region while also creating costs?
cards.answer: Remittances can support household resources, while skilled-worker loss and a changed age composition can create pressures. At destinations, migrants contribute labour but service capacity must adapt; avoid an all-good or all-bad verdict.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Make migration and urbanisation developmental.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: distinguish urban share/growth and movement → decompose urban growth → explain push–pull and agglomeration mechanisms → compare origin/destination benefits and costs → address housing, services, connectivity and participation → discuss planning and displacement trade-offs → assess inclusive productivity and living conditions.

cards.question: What depth is essential, and what should not dominate?
cards.answer: Know the urban-growth decomposition, push–pull, voluntary/forced movement, agglomeration/congestion and origin/destination trade-offs. Prepare a numerical illustration and a policy answer. Do not memorise every city model or use old urban shares; do not blame migrants inherently for service failures.

cards.question: Illustrative case: neighbourhood upgrading raises rents and displaces low-income residents. Why is physical renewal not enough?
cards.answer: The gentrification lens shows that improving buildings and attracting wealth can change living costs and community access. Assess affordability, displacement and inclusive planning alongside investment gains.
